newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says NATO chief visits Moscow next month.
newsitem.headline: Russia says NATO chief visits Moscow next month.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana will visit Moscow in late January to discuss an accord with Russia, which opposes the alliance's plans to expand eastwards, the foreign ministry said on Monday.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov earlier said dialogue between NATO and Russia was intended to assuage Moscow's anxieties about the expansion plans.
"The dialogue which is beginning with NATO is not being undertaken to change Russia's position on the expansion of NATO but to remove Russia's anxieties," he told a news conference.
"If we manage to remove these anxieties, we will move on to sign an appropriate document with NATO. If we do not, the dialogue will take on an exploratory character," he said.
Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov will meet Solana and several NATO foreign ministers in Brussels on Wednesday, a defence ministry spokesman said.

Primakov, in a key change of policy, agreed at a meeting with the 16 foreign ministers of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in Brussels earlier this month to enter a dialogue on a new relationship between the former Cold War foes.
Moscow had previously demanded that any expansion be put on ice before the start of talks on a new security partnership.
A foreign ministry spokesman said on Monday that Solana had telephoned Primakov earlier in the day to arrange the meeting.

"An agreement was reached that, in line with the proposal by NATO at the alliance's council in Brussels, the first meeting between Y. M. Primakov and J. Solana will take place in Moscow in the second half of January 1997," the spokesman said by telephone.

Primakov, in a joint news conference with Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik of Slovakia, one of the 11 countries which wants to join NATO, reiterated Moscow's opposition to expansion. Russia believes expanding NATO will lead to a new division of Europe.

"We think that it is against the interests of Russia but at the same time we do not have the right of veto and we don't impose vetoes on any NATO countries. But naturally we will fight for our interests in these conditions," he said.

NATO plans a summit in Madrid on July 8-9, when some former communist states will be invited to open membership talks. It also wants to formalise the new upgraded relationship with Russia at the same summit.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are the favourites to become NATO's first new members for more than 25 years.

But Hamzik said he told Primakov Slovakia, which borders Ukraine, Poland, Hungary, Austria and the Czech Republic, also wanted to join. "We were able to say why the Slovak Republic needs the guarantees which currently only NATO can provide," he said.
"We discussed the formation of some new security structure which would include the whole European territory," he said, adding that Slovakia sought stability with all states.
Both ministers described as positive NATO's decision at the Brussels meeting not to station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.
"The Brussels meeting demonstrated that there have been some positive changes in NATO's attitude to Russia's anxieties," Primakov said.
